title: Bangladesh gets its first self-injectable contraceptive, at Tk 550 a dose
excerpt: Incepta's Medogen SubQ gives three months' protection and can be self-administered after training. DGDA has approved it, the company says.

image.alt: A pack of combined oral contraceptive pills
image.credit: File photo: Béria Lima de Rodríguez / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

content:
Incepta Pharmaceuticals on Tuesday (24 November) launched Medogen SubQ, the first contraceptive in Bangladesh that women can inject themselves, The Business Standard and The Daily Star reported. The launch was held in Dhaka and attended by about 500 gynaecologists.

The product is a 104mg dose of medroxyprogesterone acetate injected under the skin every three months (12 to 14 weeks) using a pre-filled Uniject device. The company describes it as the first generic version of this WHO-prequalified injectable. It says each dose costs Tk 550 and that the product has been approved by the Directorate General of Drug Administration (DGDA). Women must consult a registered physician before using it.

Professor Maruf Siddiqui of the Fertility and Sterility Society of Bangladesh said it is more than 99% effective, and cited a study of 2,042 women in which no pregnancies were recorded. It can also be used to treat pain from endometriosis. Common side effects include changes in menstrual bleeding, weight gain, headache and soreness at the injection site.

Incepta chairman Abdul Muktadir said development took 13 to 14 years and cost about $60 to 70 million. He said the company is investing in local production of the active ingredient, whose price has risen from about $500 to more than $860 a kilogram.

Professor Firoza Begum, president of the Obstetrical and Gynaecological Society of Bangladesh, said training and counselling of health workers will be needed to make sure it is used correctly.

Why it matters

Injectables are widely used in Bangladesh, but women must visit a clinic or field worker every three months. A self-injectable option could help women in remote areas, garment workers and others who struggle to reach services. Whether it reaches poorer women depends on the price and on whether the government's family planning programme and NGO clinics take it up.

What to watch

Whether the Directorate General of Family Planning adds the product to its supply chain, and whether NGOs offering family planning start training women to self-inject.
